lexemes.note: Going on foot, or going to a place in general (הוֹלֵךְ לָעֲבוֹדָה). A trip by bus, car, train or plane is נָסַע. The future and the imperative lose the ה: תֵּלֵךְ, לֵךְ; infinitive לָלֶכֶת.

profile.feeling: Walking through town, going to work, going home — the first verb of movement.

senses.def: to go (to a place, in general; within a town often on foot)
to walk, go on foot
to leave, be off (אֲנִי הוֹלֵךְ “I’m off”)
to be going to (הוֹלֵךְ + infinitive: the near future)

examples.tr: We walk in the park every evening.
It’s going to be a long day.

phrases.meaning: who knows, you never can tell
there and back, a round trip (a return ticket)

synonyms.nuance: “to step, march” — measured steps; in the news and in writing (צָעַד לְאֹרֶךְ הַחוֹף “walked along the beach”)
“to stroll, go for a walk; to travel for pleasure” — walking for its own sake
not a synonym but the partner: going by bus, car, train or plane

etymology.text: From Proto-Semitic *halak- (Wiktionary). The future, the imperative and the infinitive are built as if the root were י־ל־ך: תֵּלֵךְ, לֵךְ, לָלֶכֶת.

funFacts: הֲלָכָה, Jewish religious law, comes from the same root: “the way one walks”.
A pedestrian is a הוֹלֵךְ רֶגֶל — “one who goes by foot”.
pitfalls: A trip by vehicle is נָסַע, not הָלַךְ: אֲנִי נוֹסֵעַ לְחֵיפָה “I am going to Haifa” (by bus, car, train). הָלַךְ is on foot, or going somewhere in town in general (הוֹלֵךְ לָעֲבוֹדָה).
The ה disappears in the future and the imperative: תֵּלֵךְ “you will go”, לֵךְ “go!” — and the infinitive is לָלֶכֶת.
subtleties: הוֹלֵךְ + infinitive is the colloquial “going to”: הוּא הוֹלֵךְ לִקְנוֹת “he is going to buy”, exactly as in English.
Like German gehen (on foot) vs fahren (by vehicle): הָלַךְ vs נָסַע.

lexemes.note: A hollow verb: the past and the present look alike in the masculine singular (בָּא “came” / “comes”). Imperative בּוֹא, בּוֹאִי, בּוֹאוּ; infinitive לָבוֹא.

profile.feeling: Someone on the way to you: guests, the bus, the holidays.

senses.def: to come
to come from (a place: origin)
let’s … (בּוֹא / בּוֹאוּ + a verb in the future)

examples.tr: Come to the kitchen! (to a woman)

collocations.tr: welcome (“blessed is the one who comes”)

phrases.tr: blessed is the one who comes

phrases.meaning: got on in years, was old

synonyms.nuance: “to arrive, reach” — the end of the way, not the coming itself
“to appear, show up”

etymology.text: Compare Phoenician 𐤁𐤀 (bʾ), Arabic بَاءَ (bāʔa, “to return, come back”) and Ge’ez ቦአ (boʾä, “to enter”) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: The sign at the entrance of a town or a home, בָּרוּךְ הַבָּא, uses this verb — like Greek καλώς ήρθες “well you came”.
The coming days, the next world: הָעוֹלָם הַבָּא “the world to come”.
pitfalls: The masculine singular past and present are the same word: הוּא בָּא is “he comes” or “he came” — the context decides.
The imperative has a holam: בּוֹא, בּוֹאִי, בּוֹאוּ (not *בָּא!).
subtleties: בּוֹא / בּוֹאוּ + future verb is “let’s …”: בּוֹאוּ נֵלֵךְ “let’s go”, בּוֹא נֹאכַל “let’s eat”.
Coming from somewhere is בָּא מִ…: הִיא בָּאָה מֵהָעֲבוֹדָה “she is coming from work”.

lexemes.note: A hollow verb like בָּא: רָץ “ran / runs”, רָצָה “she ran / she runs”. Do not mix it up with רָצָה “wanted” (from רָצָה, lesson 7). Infinitive לָרוּץ, imperative רוּץ.

profile.feeling: Running for the bus, jogging on the beach, children in the park.

senses.def: to run
to hurry, rush somewhere (רָץ לַשּׁוּק “dashes to the market”)
to run (in an election), be a candidate

examples.tr: The children are running in the park.
I’ll dash to the supermarket and come back.

synonyms.nuance: “to hurry” — about haste, not about running
“to gallop, race” — horses, or someone dashing

etymology.text: A hollow root ר־ו־ץ. Compare Ge’ez ሮጸ (roṣä, “to run”) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: The chess bishop is a רָץ, “runner”, like German der Läufer (Wiktionary).
A runner (athlete) is a רָץ too: the same form is also a noun.
pitfalls: רָצָה is “she runs” and “she ran” (from רָץ) and also “he wanted” (from רָצָה, lesson 7): the same letters and the same vowels — only the context (and the stress) tells them apart.
The imperative and the infinitive have וּ: רוּץ! לָרוּץ.
subtleties: רָץ לְ… with a place is “dashes to”: רָץ לַבַּנְק “dashes to the bank”.

lexemes.note: To drive (a vehicle); the driver is נֶהָג (lesson 10). The vehicle takes בְּ: נוֹהֵג בִּמְכוֹנִית. Infinitive לִנְהֹג (full spelling לנהוג).

profile.feeling: At the wheel: traffic on the motorway, a driving licence at seventeen.

senses.def: to drive (a car, a bus …)
to be in the habit of, usually do (נָהַג לְ… + infinitive)
to behave, treat (someone) in a certain way (נָהַג בְּ…)

examples.tr: She drives a bus in Tel Aviv.

examples.text: הוּא נָהַג לָשֶׁבֶת כָּאן כָּל בֹּקֶר.
examples.tr: He used to sit here every morning.

synonyms.nuance: “to drive (someone), give a lift”: הוּא מַסִּיעַ אוֹתִי לָעֲבוֹדָה — the passengers are the object
“to go by vehicle” — also as a passenger; נָהַג is only the one at the wheel

etymology.text: From the root נ־ה־ג; Wiktionary gives no further etymology. From the same root: נֶהָג “driver”, נְהִיגָה “driving”, מִנְהָג “custom” and הִתְנַהֲגוּת “behaviour” (Wiktionary).

funFacts: The same root gives מִנְהָג “custom” and הִתְנַהֲגוּת “behaviour”: the old meaning is “to lead, guide” (Wiktionary).
pitfalls: The passenger does not נוֹהֵג: אֲנִי נוֹסֵעַ בַּמּוֹנִית “I’m going by taxi”, the driver נוֹהֵג.
The vehicle takes בְּ in careful speech (נוֹהֵג בִּמְכוֹנִית); in everyday speech also a plain object: נוֹהֵג אוֹטוֹבּוּס.
subtleties: One root, three ideas: driving (נְהִיגָה), custom (מִנְהָג) and behaviour (הִתְנַהֲגוּת) — all about “leading” in a certain way.

lexemes.note: To go by vehicle and to travel. The imperative and the future lose the נ: סַע!, תִּסַּע. Infinitive לִנְסֹעַ (full spelling לנסוע).

profile.feeling: Trips and journeys: the bus to Jerusalem, the flight abroad, the summer holiday.

senses.def: to travel, go (somewhere) by vehicle
to ride, go (in a bus, a car, a train) as a passenger
to leave, set off (by vehicle): הָרַכֶּבֶת נוֹסַעַת “the train is leaving”

examples.tr: In the summer we travel to Eilat.
I (m.) go to work by bus.
The bus is leaving in a minute.

synonyms.nuance: “to travel for pleasure, tour, hike” — a trip to see places
“to sail” — by ship
“to fly” — by plane: אֲנִי טָס לְאַתּוּנָה

etymology.text: From the root נ־ס־ע (Wiktionary); related to מַסָּע “journey” and הִסִּיעַ “to give a lift” (Wiktionary). The old sense is “to pull up (the tent pegs)” — to break camp and move on.

funFacts: Wiktionary’s oldest senses of נָסַע are “to pull up” and “to remove a camp”: travellers in the desert pulled up their tent pegs to move on.
A passenger is a נוֹסֵעַ, and “Dear passengers” on an Israeli train is נוֹסְעִים יְקָרִים.
pitfalls: Going by bus, car or train is נָסַע even inside the town: אֲנִי נוֹסֵעַ לַשּׁוּק בְּאוֹטוֹבּוּס. הָלַךְ would mean you walk.
The נ falls away in the imperative and the future: סַע “go! drive!”, תִּסַּע “you will go”.
subtleties: A passenger is a נוֹסֵעַ — the same word as “travelling”.
Like German fahren: a trip by any vehicle, as driver or passenger — while נָהַג is only the driver.

lexemes.note: To come back, go back: חוֹזֵר הַבַּיְתָה “comes home”, חוֹזֵר מֵהָעֲבוֹדָה. Also “to repeat”. Infinitive לַחֲזֹר (full spelling לחזור).

profile.feeling: Coming back home in the evening, returning from a trip.

senses.def: to return, come back, go back
to repeat, do again (חָזַר עַל …)
to become religious (חָזַר בִּתְשׁוּבָה)

examples.tr: Dad comes home in the evening.
When do you (f.) come back from work?

phrases.meaning: he took it back, changed his mind

synonyms.nuance: “to return” — the Biblical and poetic word (Wiktionary lists it as a synonym)

etymology.text: From the root ח־ז־ר; Wiktionary gives no further etymology. Derived: הָלוֹךְ וְחָזוֹר “there and back” (Wiktionary).

funFacts: A school circular, a letter that “goes round”, is a חוֹזֵר — the same form of this verb.
pitfalls: “To repeat” takes עַל: חוֹזֵר עַל הַמִּלָּה “repeats the word” — without עַל it means “comes back”.
Coming home is חוֹזֵר הַבַּיְתָה — no לְ before הַבַּיְתָה.
subtleties: חוֹזֵר בִּתְשׁוּבָה “returns in repentance” means someone becomes religious; the opposite, חוֹזֵר בִּשְׁאֵלָה, someone who leaves religion.

lexemes.note: “To go in, come in”, with לְ: נִכְנָס לַחֶדֶר “goes into the room”. A nif‘al verb: the imperative and the infinitive start with הִ: הִכָּנֵס!, לְהִכָּנֵס.

profile.feeling: A door opens: come in, welcome!

senses.def: to enter, go in, come in (with לְ)
to get into (a state): נִכְנַס לְלַחַץ “got stressed”
to bump into (בְּ…): נִכְנַס בַּקִּיר “drove into the wall”

examples.tr: The teacher (f.) comes into the classroom.
Come in, the door is open. (to a man)

phrases.tr: wine went in, a secret came out
phrases.meaning: drink loosens the tongue (in vino veritas)

synonyms.nuance: “to come” — Biblical בָּא אֶל can also mean “entered”
“to penetrate, get into, break in” — with force or with difficulty

etymology.text: Nif‘al of the root כ־נ־ס “to gather, bring in”; related to הִכְנִיס “to bring in, put in” (Wiktionary). The parliament, the כְּנֶסֶת, and כְּנִיסָה “entrance” come from the same root.

funFacts: The Israeli parliament, the כְּנֶסֶת “assembly”, is from the same root כ־נ־ס.
The proverb נִכְנַס יַיִן יָצָא סוֹד uses both verbs of this lesson: wine “enters”, the secret “goes out”.
pitfalls: Entering takes לְ: נִכְנַס לַחֶדֶר “entered the room” — not *נִכְנַס בַּחֶדֶר: with בְּ the verb means “to bump into, crash into” (נִכְנַס בַּקִּיר).
The nif‘al imperative starts with הִ and doubles the first root letter: הִכָּנֵס (hikanes), not *נִכְנַס.
subtleties: In speech people say תִּכָּנֵס / תִּכָּנְסִי (the future) rather than the more formal הִכָּנֵס.
Signs say הַכְּנִיסָה אֲסוּרָה “entry is forbidden” or אֵין כְּנִיסָה “no entry”.

lexemes.note: “To go out (of), leave (a place)”, with מִ: יוֹצֵא מֵהַבַּיִת. Leaving a person or a place behind for good is עָזַב. The י falls away: צֵא!, לָצֵאת.

profile.feeling: Doors and exits: leaving the house in the morning, the train pulling out.

senses.def: to go out (of), leave, exit (with מִ)
to depart (a train, a bus, a flight)
to come out, turn out, result (הָעוּגָה יָצְאָה טוֹבָה “the cake came out well”)
to go out (in the evening), date (יוֹצֵא עִם …)

examples.tr: I (m.) leave the house in the morning.
They have been going out for a year.

phrases.tr: it came out of his nose
phrases.meaning: he was fed up with it

synonyms.nuance: “to leave (behind), quit, abandon” — for good, with אֶת: עָזַב אֶת הָעִיר
“to clear off, slip away”

etymology.text: Compare Ge’ez ወፅአ (wäṣ́ʾä), Akkadian waṣûm and Ugaritic yṣả (Wiktionary). The first root letter (originally ו) falls away in the future, the imperative and the infinitive: תֵּצֵא, צֵא, לָצֵאת.

funFacts: The Exodus is יְצִיאַת מִצְרַיִם, the “going out of Egypt” (the book itself is called שְׁמוֹת “Names”).
Idiom: יוֹצֵא דֹּפֶן, literally “coming out of the side wall”, means “exceptional” (Wiktionary).
pitfalls: Going out of a place takes מִ: יוֹצֵא מֵהַחֶדֶר. “I am leaving Tel Aviv (moving away)” is עוֹזֵב אֶת תֵּל אָבִיב.
The imperative is just צֵא — the י is gone.
subtleties: The exit is the יְצִיאָה, the way out; the entrance כְּנִיסָה — both on Israeli signs.
יָצָא also means “turned out”: יָצָא טוֹב “it came out well”.

lexemes.note: “To leave (behind)”: a place, a job, a person — for good or for a long time; the object takes אֶת: עָזַב אֶת הָעִיר. Simply going out of a room is יָצָא מִ…

profile.feeling: Goodbyes: moving out, quitting a job, leaving someone.

senses.def: to leave (a place, a job, a person), depart from
to leave alone, let be (עֲזֹב! “forget it!”)
to abandon

synonyms.nuance: “to go out (of a place)” — momentary, with מִ
“to abandon, desert” — stronger and more negative

etymology.text: From Proto-Semitic *ʕazab-; cognate with Arabic عَزَبَ (ʕazaba, “to be remote or absent”) and Akkadian ezēbum (“to leave”) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: The cognate Akkadian ezēbum also meant “to leave” — the word is older than Hebrew itself (Wiktionary).
pitfalls: עָזַב takes a direct object with אֶת: עוֹזֵב אֶת הַבַּיִת — no מִ. Going out of a room for a moment is יָצָא מֵהַחֶדֶר.
Colloquial עֲזֹב! (to a man) / עִזְבִי! (to a woman) is “forget it, never mind”, not “leave!”.
subtleties: Arabic عَزَب “unmarried” (a bachelor, “left alone”) comes from the same Semitic root (Wiktionary’s cognate عَزَبَ “to be remote or absent”).

lexemes.note: To arrive, reach; the destination takes לְ: מַגִּיעַ לַתַּחֲנָה. A hif‘il verb: present מַגִּיעַ, imperative הַגַּע (rare: people say תַּגִּיעַ).

profile.feeling: The end of the way: the bus arrives, the guests are here.

senses.def: to arrive, get to, reach (with לְ)
to be due, deserve (מַגִּיעַ לְ… “… deserves”)
to come from (origin): מַגִּיעַ מִ…

examples.tr: The bus is arriving at the stop.

synonyms.nuance: “to come” — the movement; הִגִּיעַ is the arrival
“to land” — a plane arriving: הַמָּטוֹס נָחַת

etymology.text: Hif‘il of the root נ־ג־ע “to touch”: to arrive is “to make touch, reach”. Wiktionary gives no further etymology; from the same root נָגַע “touched”.

funFacts: The root נ־ג־ע means “to touch”: arriving is “touching” the place — and מַגָּע is “contact”.
pitfalls: The destination takes לְ, not בְּ: מַגִּיעַ לַתַּחֲנָה “arrives at the stop” (German: kommt an der Haltestelle an — Hebrew says “arrives to”).
The נ of the root is hidden in a dagesh: הִגִּיעַ, מַגִּיעַ — look for נ־ג־ע.
subtleties: מַגִּיעַ לְךָ “you deserve it” — said in praise and in reproach.
The imperative הַגַּע is rare and formal; in speech say תַּגִּיעַ / תַּגִּיעִי.

lexemes.note: To stay, remain; the place takes בְּ: נִשְׁאָר בַּבַּיִת. Also “to be left (over)”. Imperative הִשָּׁאֵר, infinitive לְהִשָּׁאֵר.

profile.feeling: Staying at home on a rainy day; what is left on the plate.

senses.def: to stay, remain (somewhere)
to be left (over)

examples.tr: Today I (m.) am staying at home.

synonyms.nuance: “to stay, sojourn” — formal, about a period of time
“remained in place, unchanged”

etymology.text: Nif‘al of the root שׁ־א־ר “remain”; Wiktionary gives no further etymology. From the same root: שְׁאָר “remainder, rest” (בֵּין הַשְּׁאָר “among other things”).

funFacts: The “remnant” of Israel in the prophets is שְׁאָר / שְׁאֵרִית — the same root.
pitfalls: The place takes בְּ: נִשְׁאָר בַּבַּיִת “stays at home” (no movement, so no לְ).
The nif‘al imperative and infinitive start with הִ and double the ש: הִשָּׁאֵר, לְהִשָּׁאֵר.
subtleties: “To be left” has the thing as its subject: נִשְׁאַר לֶחֶם “bread is left”, לֹא נִשְׁאַר כְּלוּם “nothing is left”.

lexemes.note: To wait; what you wait for takes לְ: מְחַכֶּה לָאוֹטוֹבּוּס “waits for the bus”. A pi‘el verb: present מְחַכֶּה, imperative חַכֵּה, infinitive לְחַכּוֹת.

profile.feeling: Bus stops, queues, “one moment!”.

senses.def: to wait, wait for (with לְ)
to look forward to (מְחַכֶּה לְ… “can’t wait for …”)

examples.tr: I (m.) am waiting for the bus.
The children are looking forward to the holiday.

synonyms.nuance: “to wait” — formal; on the phone: נָא לְהַמְתִּין “please hold” (Wiktionary lists it as a synonym)

etymology.text: Pi‘el of the root ח־כ־ה; Wiktionary gives no further etymology and lists הִמְתִּין as its synonym.

funFacts: The recorded voice on Israeli phone lines says נָא לְהַמְתִּין — the formal partner of חִכָּה.
pitfalls: What you wait for takes לְ (not בִּשְׁבִיל): מְחַכֶּה לְאִמָּא “waiting for Mum”, לָאוֹטוֹבּוּס “for the bus”.
The ending -ֶה of the masculine present becomes -ָה in the feminine: מְחַכֶּה (m.) / מְחַכָּה (f.).
subtleties: In speech the command is mostly the future: תְּחַכֶּה רֶגַע, תְּחַכִּי רֶגַע; חַכֵּה! is shorter and sharper.
אֲנִי מְחַכֶּה לְ… also means “I’m looking forward to …”.

lexemes.role: “don’t”: the negation of commands, always followed by the future (2nd person): אַל תֵּלֵךְ “don’t go!”, אַל תְּחַכִּי “don’t wait! (to a woman)”. Never with the imperative itself (*אַל לֵךְ).

profile.feeling: Warnings and kind advice: don’t worry, don’t forget.

senses.def: don’t (+ future, 2nd person): a prohibition or a request not to do something

examples.tr: Don’t forget the key! (to a man)

phrases.text: אַל תִּסְתַּכֵּל בַּקַּנְקַן אֶלָּא בְּמַה שֶּׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹ
phrases.tr: look not at the jug but at what is in it

synonyms.nuance: with the future: a firm, lasting prohibition — the Ten Commandments say לֹא תִּגְנֹב “you shall not steal”
“it is forbidden” + infinitive: אָסוּר לְהִכָּנֵס “no entry” — on signs and for rules

etymology.text: Cognate with Phoenician 𐤀𐤋 (ʾl), Ugaritic ảl and Akkadian ul (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Arabic says “don’t” with لَا + the jussive (لَا تَذْهَبْ “don’t go”) — the same idea as Hebrew אַל + future, with another word.
pitfalls: Only with the future: אַל תֵּלֵךְ, never *אַל לֵךְ and never *לֹא לֵךְ.
Unvowelled אל is also אֶל “to” and אֵל “god” — the context decides.
subtleties: לֹא + future is a general rule or an order (“you won’t / you shall not”); אַל + future is the everyday “don’t”.

lexemes.role: “where to?” — the question word for a direction: לְאָן אַתָּה הוֹלֵךְ? “where are you going?”. (Where, at what place = אֵיפֹה; where from = מֵאֵיפֹה.)

profile.feeling: Before a trip: where to?

senses.def: where to? whither?

examples.tr: Where are you (pl.) travelling in the summer?

synonyms.nuance: “where to” in casual speech — לְאָן is the correct form

etymology.text: From לְ “to” + אָן “where” (Wiktionary). אָן alone is Biblical: עַד אָנָה “until when, how long?”.

funFacts: German keeps the same three questions apart as Hebrew: wo? (אֵיפֹה), wohin? (לְאָן), woher? (מֵאֵיפֹה).
pitfalls: With movement ask לְאָן, not אֵיפֹה: לְאָן אַתָּה נוֹסֵעַ? — like German wohin vs wo.
subtleties: Casual speech also says לְאֵיפֹה; write לְאָן.

lexemes.role: “home(wards), to the house” — one word, with no לְ: הוֹלֵךְ הַבַּיְתָה “goes home”, חוֹזֵר הַבַּיְתָה. (At home = בַּבַּיִת.)

profile.feeling: The end of the day: going home.

senses.def: home, homewards, to (one’s) home

synonyms.nuance: “to the house” — the same with the preposition; הַבַּיְתָה is the usual word for going home

etymology.text: הַבַּיִת “the house” + the old ending ־ָה “towards” (Wiktionary). The same ending is in שְׂמֹאלָה “to the left”, יָמִינָה “to the right” and הַחוּצָה “outside”.

funFacts: The ending ־ָה “towards” is a fossil of an old case ending, still alive in a few words: צָפוֹנָה “northwards”, יָמִינָה, הַבַּיְתָה.
pitfalls: No לְ before it: הוֹלֵךְ הַבַּיְתָה (not *לְהַבַּיְתָה). Being at home is בַּבַּיִת.
subtleties: The ending ־ָה is unstressed: habáyta.

profile.feeling: The green and red buses of Israeli towns, the long ride to Eilat.

senses.def: bus

examples.tr: I (m.) go to work by bus.
The bus is coming in five minutes.
Which bus goes to the central station?

synonyms.nuance: “a shuttle, transport” — a bus hired to take a group

etymology.text: An internationalism, from French autobus, coined in Paris in 1907 from “omnibus automobile”; compare Arabic أُتُوبُوس (ʔutūbūs) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Greek λεωφορείο, Turkish otobüs, Arabic أُتُوبِيس / أُتُوبُوس and Hebrew אוֹטוֹבּוּס: three of them borrowed the French autobus.
pitfalls: You get “on” a bus with עָלָה עַל: עוֹלֶה עַל הָאוֹטוֹבּוּס; you get off with יָרַד מִ: יוֹרֵד מֵהָאוֹטוֹבּוּס.
Stress on the first syllable: ótobus.
subtleties: Travelling by bus is נוֹסֵעַ בְּאוֹטוֹבּוּס (also בָּאוֹטוֹבּוּס) — never הוֹלֵךְ.

profile.feeling: The coastal train from Haifa to Tel Aviv, the fast line to Jerusalem.

senses.def: train

examples.tr: We are going to Haifa by train.

synonyms.nuance: “light rail, tram” — the city train of Jerusalem and Tel Aviv

etymology.text: Coined by Eliezer Ben-Yehuda, from the root of “riding” ר־כ־ב (Wiktionary); related to רֶכֶב “vehicle”.

funFacts: Ben-Yehuda built the word on the pattern of other “things you ride” from ר־כ־ב “to ride”: רֶכֶב “vehicle”, רַכָּב “rider”.
Arabic مَرْكَبَة “vehicle” and رَكِبَ “to ride” share the root.
pitfalls: Feminine, though it does not end in -ָה: רַכֶּבֶת מְהִירָה “a fast train” (the ending -ֶת is feminine).
The article before ר is הָ (qamats): הָרַכֶּבֶת, and so בָּרַכֶּבֶת “by train”.
subtleties: A roller coaster is a רַכֶּבֶת הָרִים, a “mountain train” (Wiktionary).

profile.feeling: Ben Gurion airport, the flight to Athens.

senses.def: aeroplane, airplane

examples.tr: We are flying to Athens in a small plane.

synonyms.nuance: the older word for “aeroplane” (Wiktionary lists it as related), now mostly in children’s language

etymology.text: From the root ט־ו־ס “to fly” (טָס “flies”) on the pattern מָקוֹם — “the flying thing”; Wiktionary gives no etymology of its own and lists אֲוִירוֹן as related.

funFacts: מָטוֹס, טִיסָה “flight” and טַיָּס “pilot” all come from ט־ו־ס “to fly”.
pitfalls: Flying is טָס, not נָסַע: אֲנִי טָס לְאַתּוּנָה “I am flying to Athens”.
The plural shortens the first vowel: מָטוֹס → מְטוֹסִים.
subtleties: A flight is a טִיסָה, from the same root: כַּרְטִיס טִיסָה “a plane ticket”.

profile.feeling: A yellow light on the roof, the meter ticking.

senses.def: taxi, cab

examples.tr: I (m.) am taking a taxi to the airport.
Take a taxi, it’s late! (to a woman)

collocations.tr: shared taxi (a minibus on a fixed route)

synonyms.nuance: the international word, heard in speech; מוֹנִית is the standard Hebrew

etymology.text: From מוֹנֶה “counter, meter” + ־ִית: a car with a meter — just as “taxi” comes from “taximeter”. Wiktionary gives no etymology of its own.

funFacts: English “taxi” is short for “taximeter”; Hebrew built its word the same way, from מוֹנֶה “meter”.
pitfalls: Feminine: הַמּוֹנִית מְחַכָּה “the taxi is waiting” (f.).
In the plural the י is doubled: מוֹנִיּוֹת (moniyot).
subtleties: A מוֹנִית שֵׁרוּת (“service taxi”, a שֵׁרוּת) is a shared minibus that runs on a fixed line, also on Shabbat in some cities.

override.N;PL;INDF: The plural of nouns in ־ִית is written with a dagesh in the י (־ִיּוֹת), as Wiktionary itself vowels מוֹנִית → מוֹנִיּוֹת; its table for מְכוֹנִית omits the dagesh.

profile.feeling: Traffic jams on the Ayalon, the family car on a Friday trip.

senses.def: car, automobile

examples.tr: My car is at the garage.

synonyms.nuance: the everyday “car” (masculine!): הָאוֹטוֹ שֶׁלִּי — Wiktionary lists it as a synonym
“vehicle” — official, in insurance and the news (רֶכֶב פְּרָטִי “private car”)

etymology.text: From מְכוֹנָה “machine” + ־ִית (Wiktionary): “the little machine”.

funFacts: German Auto, Greek αυτοκίνητο and Hebrew אוֹטוֹ: the “self-moving” car went round the world; מְכוֹנִית is Hebrew’s own “little machine”.
pitfalls: Feminine (-ִית): מְכוֹנִית חֲדָשָׁה; but the colloquial אוֹטוֹ is masculine: אוֹטוֹ חָדָשׁ.
In the plural the י is doubled: מְכוֹנִיּוֹת.
subtleties: In speech אוֹטוֹ is at least as common as מְכוֹנִית; in writing מְכוֹנִית or רֶכֶב.

lexemes.note: Only plural (a dual form, “two wheels”), masculine: הָאוֹפַנַּיִם חֲדָשִׁים “the bicycle is new”.

profile.feeling: Riding along the Tel Aviv promenade on a Saturday morning.

senses.def: bicycle, bike

examples.tr: The boy is riding a bike.
She goes to work by bike.

synonyms.nuance: not a synonym: “motorbike” — אוֹפַן + מָנוֹעַ “engine”

etymology.text: The dual of אוֹפַן “wheel” (poetic or dated), from the root א־פ־ן; coined by Eliezer Ben-Yehuda in 1903 (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Literally “a pair of wheels”: the dual ending ־ַיִם, as in עֵינַיִם “eyes” and מִשְׁקָפַיִם “glasses”.
A motorbike is an אוֹפַנּוֹעַ: אוֹפַן “wheel” + מָנוֹעַ “engine”.
pitfalls: Grammatically plural: הָאוֹפַנַּיִם שֶׁלִּי חֲדָשִׁים “my bike is new” (plural adjective).
There is no singular for “a bike”: אוֹפַן is a poetic “wheel”.
subtleties: You ride (רוֹכֵב) “on” a bike: רוֹכֵב עַל אוֹפַנַּיִם — as on a horse.

lexemes.note: A boat (small): a rowing boat, a fishing boat. A big ship is סְפִינָה (or אֳנִיָּה).

profile.feeling: Fishing boats on the Sea of Galilee, a rowing boat in the park.

senses.def: boat (small: rowing boat, motorboat, fishing boat)

examples.tr: There are boats on the Sea of Galilee.
The fisherman’s boat comes back in the morning.
We are renting a boat in the park.

synonyms.nuance: “ship” — big, seagoing
“ship” — big; the Biblical word

etymology.text: Biblical Hebrew: סִירוֹת דּוּגָה “fishing boats” (Amos 4:2); Wiktionary gives no etymology and lists אֳנִיָּה as related.

funFacts: All three water words are feminine: סִירָה, סְפִינָה and אֳנִיָּה.
pitfalls: A boat is small: a big ship is סְפִינָה or אֳנִיָּה.
Feminine: סִירָה קְטַנָּה “a small boat”.
subtleties: A boatman is a סִירַאי (Wiktionary).

lexemes.note: A ship (big). A small boat is סִירָה.

profile.feeling: Cargo ships in the port of Haifa, a cruise ship to Rhodes.

senses.def: ship, (large) boat
nave (of a church)

examples.tr: The ship leaves Haifa in the evening.
There are many ships in the port.
The nave of the church is very high.

collocations.tr: the ship of the desert (the camel)

synonyms.nuance: “ship” — the Biblical and formal word (Wiktionary lists both as related)
“boat” — small

etymology.text: Borrowed from Aramaic (sǝp̄īntā), from which Arabic سَفِينَة (safīna, “ship, vessel”) was also taken (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Arabic سَفِينَة (safīna) and Hebrew סְפִינָה are the same Aramaic word (Wiktionary).
pitfalls: A big ship: a rowing boat or a fishing boat is a סִירָה.
Before another noun it is סְפִינַת: סְפִינַת מַשָּׂא “a cargo ship”.
subtleties: סְפִינַת הַמִּדְבָּר “the ship of the desert” is the camel, as in many languages (Wiktionary).

profile.feeling: Bus cards, cinema tickets, a boarding pass.

senses.def: ticket (for a bus, train, plane, concert)
card

examples.tr: Do you (m.) have a ticket for the bus?
I (f.) am buying two train tickets.
Do you (m.) have a credit card?

synonyms.nuance: “a ticket card, a book of tickets” — several rides on one card

etymology.text: Borrowed from Ancient Greek χάρτης (khártēs) “papyrus, sheet”, from χαράσσω “I scratch, inscribe” (Wiktionary).

funFacts: From Greek χάρτης — the same word as Greek χαρτί “paper”, χάρτης “map” and English “chart”, “card”.
pitfalls: After בְּ the כּ softens: בְּכַרְטִיס (bekhartis).
A ticket “for” the bus takes לְ: כַּרְטִיס לָאוֹטוֹבּוּס, לַהַצָּגָה.
subtleties: The same word is “card”: כַּרְטִיס אַשְׁרַאי “credit card”, כַּרְטִיס בְּרָכָה “greeting card” (Wiktionary).

lexemes.note: One word: בְּ + הָ + רֶגֶל “by the foot”. הוֹלֵךְ בָּרֶגֶל “walks, goes on foot”.

profile.feeling: Short distances in town: ten minutes on foot.

senses.def: on foot

examples.tr: They come on foot from the village.

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym: בָּרֶגֶל is the everyday way to say “on foot”.

etymology.text: בְּ “in, by” + the article + רֶגֶל “foot, leg”, from Proto-Semitic *rigl- (Wiktionary lists בָּרֶגֶל among its derived terms).

funFacts: Arabic رِجْل (rijl) “foot, leg” is the same Semitic word as רֶגֶל.
The three pilgrimage festivals are the שָׁלוֹשׁ רְגָלִים, literally “three feet” — the times when people went up to Jerusalem.
pitfalls: It is one word with the article inside: בָּרֶגֶל, not *בְּרֶגֶל.
subtleties: A pedestrian is a הוֹלֵךְ רֶגֶל; “football” is כַּדּוּרֶגֶל — the same רֶגֶל (Wiktionary).
